opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the most important things academia can be doing right now, and in some ways it's a role that's become clearer as the landscape has shifted. A few years ago, a lot of academic NLP was about building systems, proposing a new architecture, getting a few points on a benchmark. The industrial labs now have such an advantage in compute and data at the frontier that if that's the only game you're playing, it's hard for a university group to compete. But I don't think that's a cause for despair, because the thing we're missing most isn't another slightly bigger model. It's an understanding of why these models work at all.

We're in this strange position where we've built artifacts that can do remarkable things, and we have very little scientific account of what's happening inside them. What kinds of representations are they building? When a model seems to know a fact or follow a chain of reasoning, what does that correspond to mechanistically? Why does it generalize in some ways and fail so badly in others? These are basic science questions, and they're the kind of questions universities are built to ask. They don't have an obvious product attached, they require patience, and the payoff often comes from careful, small, controlled experiments rather than scale.

There's also a structural reason. Academia doesn't have a commercial stake in a particular model looking good. That matters for evaluation, for interpretability, and for honestly characterizing failures. Independent researchers who can poke at these systems, publish what they find, and argue with each other in the open are a really important part of how we come to trust any scientific claim.

And I'd add that a lot of the most interesting tools come from outside computer science: linguistics, cognitive science, neuroscience. We have decades of methodology for studying a complex system whose internals we can't directly read off, which is exactly what we've been doing with human brains and minds. Universities are where those communities sit next to each other, and I think some of the best work on language models comes from bringing those perspectives together.

The one caveat is access. It's hard to do science on a model you can't look inside, so I think the health of this whole enterprise depends a lot on there being capable open models, and on some willingness from the big labs to let outside researchers study what they've built.

r001.rationale: The response says language models are remarkable artifacts for which we have “very little scientific account,” characterizing understanding as still at an early, pre-theoretical stage.

r002.rationale: It raises questions about representations, mechanisms, generalization, and failures, but does not identify finding a useful predictive theory of model behavior as an open task.

r003.rationale: It mentions small, controlled experiments and capable open models, but does not say that modest compute for inspecting open models on individual documents enables academic research.

r004.rationale: The response values basic scientific understanding, but does not assert that this value holds even if understanding is unnecessary for building future models.

r005.rationale: It draws on methods for studying human brains and minds, but does not frame language models as a way to examine how a differently constructed system can approach human cognition.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that academia's role has shifted, and we're still figuring out what it should be. For a while the implicit assumption was that we'd be the ones building the frontier systems, and that's clearly not the case anymore. The compute asymmetry is enormous, and pretending otherwise just leads to academic labs doing worse versions of industry work a year late.

But I actually think that frees us up to do the thing universities are supposed to be good at, which is science rather than engineering. If you're inside a company, your incentive is to make the next model better. You don't necessarily have the incentive, or frankly the time, to ask why the current one works. What's the actual computational mechanism by which a transformer picks up on a syntactic dependency, or tracks the state of a world described in text, or decides which of several plausible completions to produce? Those are questions where you don't need the largest model. You often learn more from a small model you can fully instrument and run a thousand experiments on.

So I see academia's job as developing the explanatory layer. We have these artifacts that behave in rich, surprising ways, and we have almost no theory connecting the training objective to the behaviors we observe. That looks a lot like the position biology was in before it had mechanisms, or psychology when it was mostly behaviorist. The interesting work is in building the intermediate concepts: what are the right units of analysis inside these networks, what counts as a representation, how do you make a claim about a model's internals that could actually be falsified.

There's also a role in being the adversarial reader. A lot of claims about what models can do come out of evaluations designed by the people who built them. Academics are well positioned to design the controlled experiments that separate genuine capability from benchmark contamination or surface heuristics. That's not glamorous, but it's a big part of how a field converges on true things.

And the last piece is training people. The students who learn to think about these systems scientifically, rather than as black boxes to be prompted, end up everywhere, including in the industry labs. That's a long-term way the academic perspective propagates even if the models themselves get built elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response says there is “almost no theory” connecting training objectives to observed behaviors and compares the field to biology before it had mechanisms.

r002.rationale: It calls for explanatory concepts and falsifiable claims about model internals, but does not identify a useful predictive theory of model behavior as an open task.

r003.rationale: It says researchers can study small, instrumentable models without the largest model, but does not mention open models or inspecting individual documents.

r004.rationale: It favors scientific inquiry over engineering, but does not clearly assert that understanding has value even if it is unnecessary for building future models.

r005.rationale: It does not frame language models as a way to investigate how a differently constructed system might approach human cognition.

astra-6.text:
I think academia has a really important role here, partly because building a capable system and understanding why it works are different research goals. You can make a model better without necessarily learning which aspects of the data, the architecture, or the training procedure were responsible. And those are exactly the kinds of questions that academic research is well positioned to pursue.

One challenge is that the largest models are expensive to train, so there are experiments that most academic labs simply can’t do. But there’s still a lot of room for carefully controlled experiments at smaller scales: varying the training data, testing specific hypotheses about what a model learns, and asking when those findings carry over to larger systems. The point isn’t just to produce a smaller version of an industrial model. It’s to design an experiment that tells us something we didn’t know before.

I also think we need to be careful about what we count as understanding. Observing that a model succeeds on a benchmark is a starting point. We’d like explanations that let us predict when it will succeed, when it will fail, and what would change its behavior. Academia can help turn this collection of impressive observations into a more systematic science.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a more systematic science, but does not characterize current understanding as pre-theoretical.

r002.rationale: It says explanations should help predict model behavior, but does not identify determining what counts as a useful predictive theory as an open task.

r003.rationale: It discusses controlled experiments at smaller scales, but not inspecting open models on individual documents.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes building capable systems from understanding them, but does not assert that understanding has intellectual value even if unnecessary for future model building.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss comparing language models with human cognition or how closely differently constructed systems can approach it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academia has a really important role to play in asking what these systems are doing and why they work. There’s a tremendous amount of progress in building more capable models, but that doesn’t automatically give us a scientific understanding of them. What have they learned from their training data? What kinds of representations do they build? When should we expect them to generalize, and when should we expect them to fail?

One thing universities can contribute is the freedom to study those questions without needing every experiment to produce a better product. Sometimes that means working with smaller models or more controlled datasets, where you can change one thing at a time and distinguish between competing explanations. You need to connect those experiments back to the larger systems, but there’s real value in having settings where you can actually figure out what caused a particular behavior.

And I think this is a place where connections to linguistics, cognitive science, and other fields can be useful. We have a lot of tools for thinking about language and learning already. The opportunity is to turn observations about what language models can do into explanations that make predictions—and then test those predictions.

r001.rationale: The response says progress in building models does not automatically provide scientific understanding, but does not characterize the field as pre-theoretical.

r002.rationale: It proposes developing and testing predictive explanations, but does not identify deciding what makes a predictive theory useful as an open scientific task.

r003.rationale: It mentions smaller models and controlled datasets, but not the low computational cost of inspecting open models on individual documents.

r004.rationale: It values research that need not improve a product, but does not state that scientific understanding has intellectual value even if it is unnecessary for building future language models.

r005.rationale: The response does not frame language models as a way to investigate how closely systems built very differently from humans can approach human cognition.
